lines.say: Here's a question. When you measure ten qubits, how many different results could you see?
Picture a combination lock where every wheel has just two positions, zero and one.
One wheel gives two settings. Add a second wheel, and now there are four.
Zero zero, zero one, one zero, and one one.
A third wheel makes eight, and every new wheel doubles the count again.
So ten wheels give two to the power of ten, which is one thousand and twenty four.
Qubits count the same way. Ten qubits have one thousand and twenty four possible results.
Here's the quantum part. Qubits keep a number for every one of those results, called an amplitude.
Each amplitude sets how likely its result is, so ten qubits carry one thousand and twenty four of them.
That doubling with every qubit is where a quantum computer gets its room to work.
But here the lock picture breaks. A lock is only ever set to one combination.
Qubits carry an amplitude for every combination, yet measuring them shows you just one.
So all those amplitudes don't mean all those answers. You get one string of ten zeros and ones.
One last habit to lock in. When Kiss kit writes a string, qubit zero goes on the right.
Take two qubits, and flip only qubit zero to one.
Kiss kit shows zero one, not one zero, like a number whose smallest place sits on the right.
So every qubit you add doubles the amplitudes, but a measurement still shows you just one string.
